author: ROAPE
title: African Labour and Liberation
content:
African Labour and Liberation

 brings together the experiences of workers, trade unions and labour movements across the continent to ask what they can tell us about work, power and liberation today. We assembled this collection because of the surprisingly few recent accounts of the emergence of a class politics on the continent. Labour is central to understanding the present political economy of Africa.  More than 90 percent of Africa’s 500 million workers work in informal and precarious jobs in a labour force that will grow rapidly in the next three decades.




The social and political mobilization of workers in multifarious contexts across the continent is imperative to improving their socio-economic conditions. It is necessary to situate Africa’s workers at the centre. This collection starts from the premise that labour struggles are essential to improving the conditions of work and stamping out poverty and inequality that the confronts most African workers today and form the basis for building new forms of collective power.




This heterodox collec­tion finds six primary patterns prevalent in the struggle for the working class liberation in the post-independence era.

author: ROAPE
title: Fanon’s continuing presence and revolutionary Sudan
content:
Each generation must out of relative obscurity discover its mission, fulfil it, or betray it.




– Frantz Fanon, 

The Wretched of the Earth

, 1968




I do not come with timeless truths … Every human problem must be considered from the standpoint of time.




– Frantz Fanon, 

Black Skin, White Masks

, 2008




 




Introduction




Fanon was very aware of his time. And yet one hundred years after his birth, he remains strangely present, as if we are repeating the same history, the long durée of the unfinished anticolonial revolutions (see Gibson 2021). Published in 1961, Fanon’s last book, 

The Wretched of the Earth

, is a product of his experience and reflections on Africa’s anticolonial struggle, including its first crisis in the Congo in 1961. Written as an intervention and addressing the readers as comrades, Fanon introduces the colonised challenge to the colonial world not as a rational confrontation of points of view, ‘but the untidy affirmation of an original idea propounded as an absolute’ (Fanon 1968, 41). Aware that colonialism carved up the continent into colonial fiefdoms, Fanon recognised that while the social struggle takes on a national form, it would inevitably degenerate into the regional, ethnic and racial lines often promulgated by colonial rule 

if

author: ROAPE
title: What is the Real Marxist Tradition in Africa?
content:
John Molyneux’s classic statement of Marxist theory and practice 

What is the Real Marxist Tradition

? was first published in 1984. The short book provided an incredibly sophisticated description of Marx’s method, and his relentless and insistent focus on the core agency of the working class.




Only the working class – however it is interpreted, described or labelled in social theory – can deliver a revolutionary anti-capitalist project. There cannot be, Molyneux argued, any substitute – no enlightened project of state development, or ‘socialist’ military leadership who deliver socialism on behalf of working people. Molyneux – in restating Marx’s central tenet – emphasised the role of the working class in their self-emancipation. Marx was the original prophet of the self-emancipation by working people. Without this class, and this project, there is simply no Marxism, no socialism, and no possibility of international revolution.




For an African audience the book speaks to multiple failed projects of socialism delivered by military coups, ‘enlightened’ governments and guerrilla movements. Each of these movements at different times dressed themselves in the language of Marxism, class and anti-imperialism but systematically broke genuine efforts at working class power.

author: ROAPE
title: The price of becoming your own boss in Uganda’s boda boda industry
content:
It is said that Uganda’s vast motorcycle-taxi industry employs more men than any other sector outside agriculture. In Kampala alone, Uganda’s rapidly expanding capital city, estimates suggests there could be upwards of 

300,000 moto-taxi

 (or 

boda boda

) drivers currently in circulation out of a daytime population of roughly four million workers and residents. Moving people and things from A to B is big business here – and there is big business too in the alleviation of 

boda

 driver hardships.




Fuelled by global venture capital and facilitated by both 

digital technologies

 and 

loose

 

regulatory

 oversight, over the past 15 years a new regime of 

‘for-profit poverty reduction’

 has coursed its way through the highways and back alleys of this thriving sector. Through Buy Now, Pay Later credit products targeted specifically towards the 

boda

 market, a growing fleet of specialist asset financing companies offer drivers the chance to escape a long-running informal rental system (known locally as 

kibaluwa

) by one day acquiring a motorcycle of their own. Or to use the aspirational phrasing of one of Uganda’s largest moto-taxi financiers, Tugende, to 

‘be their own boss’

.

author: ROAPE
title: Food security or seed capture? The colonial potato and Africa’s seed wars
content:
It all begins with a potato. Not the kind that nourishes a nation in textbook stories, but a colonial potato. This potato was shipped, tested, rationed, pushed through mission gardens and military supply lines, and ultimately sold as progress. Tracing that potato across Nigeria’s highlands leads to today’s disputes over seed, debt, law, and who decides what African farmers cultivate. 




Seeds are not just seeds. They carry memory, labour, taste, law, power, and often, debt. 

The colonial potato scheme in Nigeria

 is significant because it shows how dependency on seeds can develop even before it is codified in law. Nowadays, discussions about seed sovereignty in Africa often centre on patents, plant breeders’ rights, certified seed laws, and agribusiness. However, colonial Nigeria reveals an older method of control: emergency.       




In the 1930s and 1940s, British officials transformed the 

Jos and Mambila Plateaus

 into experimental sites for growing potatos. Initially, the scheme was small and awkward, driven by European miners, missionaries, and colonial officers seeking familiar food. Then, the Second World War (1939-1945) changed everything. Supply routes were disrupted, troops needed food, and Nigerian highland farmers were forcibly integrated into a larger imperial food plan. An agricultural experiment became part of the British empire’s war effort.
